what_impresses: The real-time world map with animated flow dots along shipping routes, region-based color coding, tier-based route opacity, and clickable port detail is genuinely impressive for a demo
The pipeline architecture diagram with clickable nodes, animated data flow arrows, feedback loop SVG, and right-hand detail panel is a creative and informative way to visualize a multi-agent system
Presentation mode and demo auto-cycle mode show forethought about actual demo scenarios that many production dashboards lack
WebSocket reconnection with exponential backoff (5 retries, capped at 30s) is production-grade network handling
The service funnel pyramid with GA and MILP stages is an excellent way to communicate optimization pipeline performance to non-technical stakeholders
Footer status bar showing pipeline, GA, MILP, and coverage status at a glance matches real operations center standards
5-region color scheme with consistent application across map, cards, charts, and pipeline views shows strong design system thinking
Benchmark targets (weekly profit $500M, 70% coverage, 20% margin, 450 services) with badge indicators add accountability to KPI cards
what_confuses: Two entirely separate dashboard implementations exist: LiveDashboard.jsx (zustand store, simple white theme in parts) and MaritimeDashboard.jsx (comprehensive dark terminal theme). It is unclear which is the canonical app.

The views/ folder contains framer-motion-only components (FunnelView, FeedbackView, ConflictView, SummaryView, RegionalView) that use hardcoded demo data, but these are NOT the same as the live-data versions embedded in MaritimeDashboard.jsx. A developer reading the views/ folder would get the wrong impression.

The ui/Counter.jsx component animates entrance only (framer-motion scale+opacity) while the inline Counter function in MaritimeDashboard.jsx does actual step-counting animation. These share a name but have completely different behavior.
The index.css font-family declaration specifies system-ui sans-serif, while the actual app components render everything in Courier New monospace. The CSS and the JSX contradict each other.

MapView.jsx in the views/ folder is an emoji placeholder, while the real interactive map is defined inline inside MaritimeDashboard.jsx alongside all other views. This makes the directory structure misleading.

production_gaps.gap: Two competing dashboard implementations (LiveDashboard.jsx vs MaritimeDashboard.jsx) with different state management patterns and styling systems
Export button renders a fake canvas with hardcoded text instead of capturing the actual DOM content
Views folder contains dead code with hardcoded demo data that could mislead future developers
Zero accessibility features: no aria-labels, no keyboard navigation for map, no focus indicators, no screenreader support
No mobile or tablet responsive support; dashboard is effectively desktop-only
Multiple 60fps setInterval animation loops running continuously even when pipeline is idle, risking battery drain and CPU usage
Counter component has two completely different implementations with the same name but different behavior
Font sizes as low as 6px used for labels will be illegible on standard-resolution displays
No loading skeleton states or optimistic UI for WebSocket data arriving asynchronously
Map lacks zoom and pan controls for a global geographic visualization

overall_assessment: The Liner Shipping Optimizer dashboard is a visually impressive demo piece that successfully communicates a complex multi-agent optimization pipeline through creative visualization choices: the animated maritime map, the architectural pipeline diagram with clickable nodes, the service funnel pyramid, and the convergence trajectory chart all work together to tell a compelling story. The dark terminal aesthetic with cyan accents and scanline overlay evokes Bloomberg Terminal and will impress during a demo. However, the codebase reveals significant production-readiness concerns. Two parallel dashboard implementations (LiveDashboard.jsx and MaritimeDashboard.jsx) create confusion about which is canonical. The views/ folder contains dead-code components with hardcoded demo data that are disconnected from the WebSocket. The export button is non-functional, accessibility is essentially absent, and the dashboard has no responsive support outside desktop viewports. The 6px and 7px font sizes used throughout will be illegible on standard-resolution monitors. For a demo to technical stakeholders or investors, this will score highly due to the visual polish and real-time streaming capabilities. For production deployment to actual operations teams, significant work remains: consolidating the duplicate implementations, implementing proper export, adding accessibility, and supporting non-desktop viewports. The component duplication and hardcoded demo data in the views directory represent the highest-priority architectural debt, as they will actively mislead any new developer joining the project.
